questions.q: A baby born to an HIV-positive mother tests positive for HIV antibodies at birth, though the baby may not be infected. This is because:
o: Antibodies from the mother cross the placenta into the baby's blood
The baby has already made antibodies in the womb in every case
HIV antibodies are inherited through the mother's genes
The test always gives a false result in newborns
questions.x: Maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and stay in the baby's blood for many months, so an antibody test cannot tell whether the baby itself is infected.

questions.q: The genetic material of poliovirus is:
questions.x: Poliovirus is a small naked RNA virus with a single strand of RNA. Double-stranded DNA is found in viruses such as herpes, adeno- and poxviruses.

questions.q: Viruses such as rabies virus and poliovirus, which mainly attack the nervous system, are described as:
questions.x: Classified by the tissue they attack, viruses that target nerves are neurotropic. Dermotropic viruses attack the skin, pneumotropic the lungs, and viscerotropic the internal organs such as the liver.

questions.q: The correct order in which electrons pass along the electron transport chain is:
o: NADH → flavoprotein (FAD) → coenzyme Q → cytochromes → oxygen
questions.x: Electrons from NADH pass to a flavoprotein, then to coenzyme Q, then down the cytochromes and finally to oxygen, which is the last acceptor.

questions.q: The RQ of yeast respiring glucose completely anaerobically is:
o: Zero, because no carbon dioxide is released
Very high (infinite), because carbon dioxide is released while no oxygen is used
questions.x: In alcoholic fermentation carbon dioxide is produced but no oxygen is taken in, so the ratio CO2 ÷ O2 has a zero denominator and is very large.

questions.q: Hair is made of α-keratin, whose polypeptide chains are mainly folded into:
questions.x: In α-keratin, each polypeptide coils into an alpha helix, and several helices twist together into tough fibres. Beta pleated sheets are typical of silk fibroin.

questions.q: Complete hydrolysis of a nucleoprotein such as chromatin would yield:
o: Fatty acids, glycerol and amino acids
Amino acids, glucose and fatty acids
Amino acids, a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and nitrogenous bases
questions.x: The protein part gives amino acids. The nucleic acid part breaks down into its nucleotide components: a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and nitrogenous bases.

questions.q: Hydrogen bonds in biological molecules differ from covalent bonds in that hydrogen bonds are:
o: Much weaker and easily broken and re-formed
Much stronger and very hard to break
Formed by complete transfer of electrons
questions.x: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a partly positive hydrogen and a partly negative atom such as oxygen or nitrogen, so it breaks and re-forms easily. Covalent bonds involve shared electrons and are much stronger.

questions.q: A DNA template strand contains 20% adenine, 30% thymine, 25% guanine and 25% cytosine. What percentage of the mRNA copied from it is uracil?
questions.x: Uracil is placed opposite each adenine of the template, so the mRNA has as much uracil as the template has adenine: 20%. Template thymine pairs with adenine in the mRNA.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes fats from oils?
o: Fats are solid at room temperature, while oils are liquid
Fats contain glycerol, while oils do not
Oils contain ester bonds, while fats do not
Fats come only from plants, while oils come only from animals
questions.x: Fats and oils are both triglycerides with glycerol and ester bonds. Fats (mostly animal) are solid at room temperature, and oils (mostly plant) are liquid.

questions.q: Codons on mRNA are read one after another with no gaps or punctuation between them. This property of the code is described as:
questions.x: A commaless code has no spacer bases between codons, so reading runs continuously from the start codon. Degenerate means several codons for one amino acid.

questions.q: Fat in the diet is needed for the absorption of vitamins:
questions.x: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and are absorbed along with dietary fat. The B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble.

questions.q: Phospholipids are described as amphipathic because each molecule:
o: Can act as both an acid and a base
Dissolves equally well in water and in ether
Has both a water-attracting part and a water-repelling part
questions.x: Amphipathic means having both a hydrophilic part (the phosphate head) and a hydrophobic part (the fatty acid tails). This is why phospholipids form bilayers in water.

questions.q: The sequence of amino acids in a protein is ultimately determined by:
o: The number of disulphide bonds in the protein
The amount of water in the cell
The sequence of nucleotides in a gene
questions.x: A gene's base sequence codes for the order of amino acids. Disulphide bonds and conditions such as temperature affect shape, not the sequence.

questions.q: Elastin, a protein found in the walls of arteries and in the lungs, allows these tissues to:
questions.x: Elastin fibres can be stretched and spring back, so arteries and lungs return to shape. Active contraction depends on actin and myosin, and clotting on fibrin.

questions.q: Different forms of the same gene, found at the same locus, are called:
questions.x: Alleles are alternative versions of a gene at the same position on homologous chromosomes. Codons and anticodons are base triplets, and chromatids are copies of a chromosome.

questions.q: The type of RNA whose bases are read in groups of three, called codons, is:
questions.x: Codons are triplets on mRNA that specify amino acids. tRNA carries the complementary anticodon, and rRNA forms part of the ribosome.

questions.q: The endoplasmic reticulum exists in three forms, which are:
questions.x: ER is a network of flattened sacs (cisternae), branching tubules and small vesicles. Grana and stroma belong to chloroplasts; cristae and matrix to mitochondria.

questions.q: Which of the following organisms has eukaryotic cells?
questions.x: Yeast is a unicellular fungus with a true nucleus. E. coli and Streptococcus are bacteria and Nostoc is a cyanobacterium, all prokaryotes.

questions.q: The DNA and ribosomes of a mitochondrion are found in its:
questions.x: The matrix contains circular mitochondrial DNA, 70S ribosomes and the enzymes of the Krebs cycle.

questions.q: Under the electron microscope, a cell shows a nucleus with a double envelope, mitochondria, 80S ribosomes and a cell wall made of chitin. The cell belongs to a:
questions.x: A nucleus, mitochondria and 80S ribosomes mark a eukaryote; a chitin wall shows it is a fungus. Plants have cellulose walls and animals have no wall.

questions.q: During depolarisation, Na+ ions enter the axon by:
o: Active transport by the sodium–potassium pump
Diffusion down their concentration and electrical gradients through open channels
questions.x: Na+ is more concentrated outside and the inside is negative, so Na+ diffuses in passively once its channels open. The pump moves Na+ outwards, not in.

questions.q: Immediately after one action potential, the concentrations of Na+ and K+ inside the axon have:
o: Reversed, with more Na+ than K+ inside
Changed only very slightly, because few ions cross the membrane
questions.x: Only a tiny fraction of the ions cross during one impulse, which is enough to change the voltage but barely alters concentrations. The pump later restores them.

questions.q: At rest, K+ ions slowly leave the neuron mainly through:
o: Potassium leak channels that stay open
questions.x: Leak channels let K+ diffuse out at rest, which helps make the inside negative. The pump moves K+ inwards, not out.

questions.q: Which function belongs to the cerebrum and NOT to the cerebellum?
o: Conscious perception of sensations such as pain
questions.x: Sensations become conscious in the sensory areas of the cerebral cortex. Posture, balance and smooth coordination of movements are the work of the cerebellum.

questions.q: Synaptic knobs contain many mitochondria. This is because the knobs need:
o: Oxygen to store in their vesicles
ATP for making and releasing neurotransmitter
questions.x: Synthesis of transmitter and its release by exocytosis need energy, supplied as ATP by the mitochondria.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the ion distribution of a resting neuron?
o: K+ is more concentrated inside and Na+ is more concentrated outside
Na+ is more concentrated inside and K+ outside
Na+ and K+ are equally concentrated on both sides
Both Na+ and K+ are more concentrated inside
questions.x: The pump keeps Na+ high outside and K+ high inside. These gradients make the resting potential and action potential possible.

questions.q: Impulses from touch receptors in the hand are passed on in which part of the forebrain before reaching the sensory area of the cortex?
questions.x: Sensory impulses from the body are relayed in the thalamus, which passes them to the sensory area of the parietal lobe. The hypothalamus regulates internal conditions.

questions.q: Structurally, most thermoreceptors of the skin are:
o: Capsules of concentric connective tissue layers
questions.x: Skin thermoreceptors are free nerve endings. Concentric capsules describe Pacinian corpuscles, rod-shaped cells are in the retina and hair cells are in the inner ear.

questions.q: Pepsin digests proteins by hydrolysing their:
questions.x: Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, which proteases such as pepsin break with water. Glycosidic bonds link sugars and ester bonds occur in fats.

questions.q: Enzymes that join small molecules into larger ones during synthesis usually do so by:
questions.x: Building large molecules such as proteins and polysaccharides involves condensation reactions, in which a molecule of water is removed at each bond formed.

questions.q: Which of the following is an intracellular enzyme?
questions.x: Glycolytic enzymes act inside the cell, in the cytoplasm. Pepsin, pancreatic lipase and salivary amylase are secreted and act outside the cells that make them.

questions.q: Which statement about cofactors is correct?
o: All cofactors are permanently bound to their enzymes
A cofactor may be an inorganic ion or an organic molecule
All cofactors are made of RNA
questions.x: Cofactors are non-protein helpers: inorganic ions such as Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺, or organic molecules (coenzymes and prosthetic groups). Some are loose, others tightly bound.

questions.q: The catalytic action of an enzyme's active site is mainly due to:
o: The peptide bonds of the whole enzyme
The side chains (R groups) of particular amino acids lining it
Phosphate groups attached to the enzyme
Water molecules trapped in the enzyme
questions.x: The R groups of the active-site amino acids give it its shape and chemical properties, which hold the substrate and help break or form its bonds.

questions.q: Lamarck published his theory in 1809 and Darwin's On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859. How many years separate the two?
questions.x: 1859 − 1809 = 50 years. Lamarck's theory therefore came half a century before Darwin's.

questions.q: Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle lasted about:
questions.x: The voyage lasted from 1831 to 1836, about five years, much of it surveying the coasts of South America.

questions.q: Lamarck believed that living things have an inner tendency to:
o: Stay the same as when they were first created
Produce far more offspring than can survive
Become more complex and better suited over time
Lose all organs that are used often
questions.x: Lamarck thought organisms had an inbuilt drive towards greater complexity, together with use and disuse and inheritance of acquired characters. Overproduction was Darwin's postulate.

questions.q: When gonorrhoea causes symptoms in a woman, they may include:
o: Vaginal discharge and pain on passing urine
A rash on the palms and soles
questions.x: Women with gonorrhoea may have a vaginal discharge and painful urination, though many have no symptoms. A painless ulcer suggests syphilis; blisters suggest herpes.

questions.q: In an outbreak of genital herpes, the typical sequence of the skin lesions is:
o: A painless hard ulcer forms and lasts for years
A rash on the palms spreads to the whole body
Small blisters form, burst into painful ulcers, then crust and heal
Warts grow slowly and never heal
questions.x: Herpes blisters (vesicles) rupture to leave painful shallow ulcers that crust over and heal in one to two weeks; the virus then becomes latent.

questions.q: The soft, destructive, tumour-like lesions that may appear in the skin, bones or organs in tertiary syphilis are called:
questions.x: Gummas are typical of tertiary syphilis. A chancre is the painless ulcer of the primary stage, and vesicles are the blisters of herpes.

questions.q: Which distance in a sarcomere stays the same during contraction?
o: From one Z line to the next Z line
From the M line to the tip of a thick filament
From a Z line to the nearest edge of the A band
Across the width of the H zone
questions.x: The M line to the tip of a thick filament is half the A band, and it stays constant because thick filaments do not shorten. Z line to Z line, the half I band and the H zone all shrink as thin filaments slide in.

questions.q: The biceps and triceps are called an antagonistic pair because they:
o: Always contract at the same time
Produce opposite movements at the same joint
Are made of different types of muscle
questions.x: Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs: the biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it. Both are skeletal muscles, and they contract alternately, not together.

questions.q: Both the shoulder and the hip are ball-and-socket joints, yet the hip is more stable. This is mainly because the hip has:
o: A shallow socket that allows more movement
A deep socket that holds the femur's head firmly
Fibrous tissue in place of synovial fluid
questions.x: The deep acetabulum and strong ligaments hold the femur securely, giving stability for weight bearing. The shoulder's shallow glenoid cavity allows more movement but dislocates more easily.

questions.q: A person straightens the arm at the elbow. Which statement is correct?
o: The biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes
The triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes
The biceps pushes the forearm downwards
questions.x: Extension of the elbow is produced by contraction of the triceps, while its antagonist, the biceps, relaxes. Muscles cannot push; they only pull.

questions.q: A student lists features of cartilage tissue. Which one is right?
o: Its matrix is hardened by calcium phosphate
Its matrix contains no blood vessels or nerves
Its cells are linked by canaliculi
Its matrix is arranged in Haversian systems
questions.x: Cartilage is avascular and has no nerves; its cells get nutrients by diffusion through the matrix. Calcium phosphate hardening, canaliculi and Haversian systems all belong to bone.

questions.q: The biceps arises from the scapula and is inserted on the radius. When the biceps contracts:
o: The elbow straightens as the forearm is lowered
The scapula is pulled down towards the forearm
The elbow bends as the forearm is raised
questions.x: A muscle pulls its insertion towards its origin. The biceps pulls the radius up towards the shoulder, so the elbow bends (flexion). Straightening the elbow is done by the triceps.

questions.q: The elbow joint is formed where the lower end of the humerus meets the upper ends of the:
questions.x: At the elbow the humerus meets the ulna (the main hinge) and the radius. Tibia and fibula are leg bones, and scapula and clavicle form the shoulder girdle.

questions.q: The fluid matrix that surrounds the myofibrils, mitochondria and glycogen granules inside a muscle cell is named:
questions.x: The cytoplasm of a muscle fibre is the sarcoplasm; it holds the myofibrils, mitochondria and glycogen. The sarcolemma is the cell membrane, and the sarcomere is the contractile unit of a myofibril.

questions.q: Mendel's law of dominance states that:
o: The two alleles of a gene separate when gametes are formed
Alleles of different genes enter gametes independently of each other
When two contrasting alleles are present together, only one of them is expressed in the phenotype
Genes on the same chromosome are inherited together
questions.x: The law of dominance says that in a hybrid only one of the two contrasting factors (the dominant one) shows. Separation of alleles is the law of segregation, and independent entry of different genes is the law of independent assortment.

questions.q: A person has 44 autosomes and a single X chromosome (XO). This person develops as:
questions.x: Without a Y chromosome the body develops as female (Turner's syndrome, usually sterile). This shows that the Y, not the number of X chromosomes, causes maleness.

questions.q: A dihybrid is produced by crossing AAbb with aaBB, and the two genes are linked. In its test cross, which offspring will be the rare recombinants?
o: AaBb (both dominant traits) and aabb (both recessive)
Aabb (trait A only) and aaBb (trait B only)
AaBb and Aabb (all showing trait A)
aaBb and aabb (all lacking trait A)
questions.x: The dihybrid received Ab from one parent and aB from the other, so it is in repulsion. Its new combinations are AB and ab, giving AaBb and aabb offspring.

questions.q: The ABO blood group is controlled by three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i). How many different genotypes are possible?
questions.x: The genotypes are IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi, IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi, IᴬIᴮ and ii, which is 6. Four is the number of blood group phenotypes (A, B, AB, O).

questions.q: From the cross XᵂXʷ × XʷY in Drosophila, the fraction of white-eyed flies expected among all the progeny is:
questions.x: XᵂXʷ × XʷY gives XᵂXʷ, XʷXʷ, XᵂY and XʷY in equal numbers. White-eyed females and white-eyed males together make 1/2.

questions.q: All the genes carried on one chromosome together form a:
questions.x: The genes of one chromosome make up a linkage group. A genome is the whole set of genes, a gene pool is all the genes of a population, and a karyotype is the chromosome set as seen in a picture.

questions.q: An X-linked recessive trait often seems to skip a generation because it is passed on through:
o: Sons who carry it on their Y chromosome
Carrier daughters who do not show the trait
Affected fathers to all their sons
questions.x: An affected man's daughters are carriers with normal phenotype; the trait then reappears in about half of their sons.

questions.q: If Xʰ is the hemophilia allele, a man with hemophilia has the genotype:
questions.x: The hemophilia gene is on the X only, so an affected man has one Xʰ and a Y. XᴴY is a normal man.

questions.q: In the villi, digested fats enter the lacteals mainly as:
o: Tiny fat droplets coated with protein (chylomicrons)
questions.x: Fatty acids and glycerol are rebuilt into fat inside intestinal cells and leave as protein-coated droplets (chylomicrons), which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the lacteals.

questions.q: Each semilunar valve of the human heart is made of:
o: Two flaps held by chordae tendineae
Four flaps held by papillary muscles
questions.x: Semilunar valves have three pocket-shaped (half-moon) cusps and no chordae tendineae. Flaps tied by chordae tendineae belong to the atrioventricular valves.

questions.q: Small arteries branch into still smaller vessels that lead into the capillaries. These vessels are:
questions.x: Arteries divide into arterioles, which feed capillaries. Venules collect blood from the capillaries and join to form veins.

questions.q: Normal lymph from the arms and legs is:
questions.x: Lymph is a clear, pale fluid because it has no red blood cells. Only lymph from the gut after a fatty meal (chyle) looks milky.

questions.q: The space in the thorax between the two lungs, in which the heart lies, is called the:
questions.x: The heart sits in the mediastinum, the central region of the thorax between the lungs. The pleural cavities surround the lungs, and the peritoneal cavity is in the abdomen.

questions.q: Specific defence, which develops during life after contact with particular antigens, is also called:
questions.x: Specific defence is acquired or adaptive: it develops after exposure to a particular antigen or vaccine. Innate, non-specific defences are present from birth and act the same way against all invaders.

questions.q: In active immunity, the antibodies that protect the person are:
o: Received from another person or an animal
Received only from the mother's milk
Made by that person's own lymphocytes
questions.x: Active immunity means the person's own B cells respond and make antibodies, which also produces memory cells. Antibodies received from another source give passive immunity.

questions.q: Smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease mainly because substances in smoke:
o: Make the heart muscle grow stronger
Damage the lining of arteries, encouraging fatty deposits (atheroma) to build up
questions.x: Nicotine and carbon monoxide damage the inner lining of arteries, making fatty plaques more likely to form and narrow the coronary arteries. Nicotine also raises blood pressure and makes clotting more likely, not less.

questions.q: During normal expiration, the diaphragm:
o: Relaxes and returns to its upward dome shape
Stays flat and does not move
questions.x: In expiration the diaphragm muscle relaxes and is pushed back up into its dome shape by the abdominal organs, reducing the volume of the thorax. It is during inspiration that it contracts and flattens.

questions.q: Of a normal 500 mL breath, about 150 mL only fills the nose, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles, where no gas exchange takes place. This volume is called the:
questions.x: The conducting airways hold about 150 mL of air that never reaches the alveoli; this is the anatomical dead space. Residual volume is the air left in the lungs after a maximal expiration.

questions.q: Many long-term smokers make a whistling sound (wheeze) when breathing out. Wheezing is caused by:
o: Air leaking into the pleural cavity
Vibration of the vocal cords during expiration
Air flowing through narrowed bronchi and bronchioles
questions.x: When inflammation, thick mucus and muscle spasm narrow the airways, air rushing through them makes a whistling wheeze, especially on breathing out. The vocal cords produce speech, not wheeze.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the large intestine with the small intestine?
o: It is longer and narrower, with more villi
It is wider and longer, with larger villi
It is narrower but shorter, and secretes more enzymes
It is wider but shorter, and its lining has no villi
questions.x: The large intestine is only about 1.5 m long but wider in diameter. Its lining has no villi and secretes mucus rather than digestive enzymes.

questions.q: Starch that escapes digestion in the mouth is digested mainly in the small intestine by:
questions.x: Pancreatic juice contains amylase, which continues breaking starch into maltose in the duodenum. Pepsin and rennin act on proteins, and lipase on fats.

questions.q: The control of ADH secretion, in which the effect of the hormone removes its own stimulus, is an example of:
questions.x: A concentrated blood triggers ADH; ADH saves water and dilutes the blood, which then reduces ADH release. A response that cancels its own stimulus is negative feedback.

questions.q: Because hydrogen ions are secreted into the kidney tubules, normal human urine is usually:
questions.x: Secretion of H+ removes acid from the blood, so urine is usually slightly acidic, around pH 6. Its pH varies with diet but it is never as acidic as gastric juice.

questions.q: A patient whose kidneys work at only a small fraction of normal (end-stage kidney failure) needs, to survive:
o: Regular dialysis or a kidney transplant
questions.x: At end stage the kidneys can no longer keep the blood clean, so either dialysis or a transplanted kidney must take over their work.

questions.q: Exchange of substances between the tubule cells and the peritubular capillaries takes place through the:
questions.x: Tubule cells move reabsorbed materials into the surrounding tissue fluid, from which they enter the capillaries; secreted substances take the reverse route.

questions.q: In a kidney transplant, the ureter of the donor kidney is joined to the patient's:
questions.x: The new kidney's ureter drains urine into the bladder, just as a natural ureter does.

questions.q: Although most solutes are reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, the fluid leaving it is still isotonic to blood plasma. This is because:
o: No water is reabsorbed in this part
Urea is secreted to replace the lost solutes
Water is reabsorbed in proportion with the solutes
Plasma proteins enter the tubule there
questions.x: In the PCT water follows the reabsorbed solutes by osmosis, so volume falls greatly but concentration stays the same as plasma. The fluid becomes hypertonic or hypotonic only in the loop of Henle and later.

questions.q: In the ornithine cycle, citrulline is converted into arginine by gaining:
questions.x: Ornithine first takes up one ammonia (with carbon dioxide) to form citrulline; citrulline then gains a second nitrogen to form arginine. This explains why urea has two nitrogen atoms.

questions.q: A patient with a stone stuck in the ureter develops fever and chills. This most likely means that:
o: Urine trapped above the stone has become infected
The kidney is making extra urine
The stone has passed into the bladder
questions.x: Urine that cannot drain becomes a site for bacterial growth, and the infection causes fever. A passed or dissolved stone would relieve the problem.

questions.q: A beaver living in fresh water has kidneys with mostly short loops of Henle. This suits it because it:
o: Has plenty of water and does not need to make concentrated urine
Must make urine more concentrated than a desert rat's
Has no need to filter its blood
Loses water mainly through its lungs
questions.x: Long loops build the medullary salt gradient needed for concentrated urine. An animal surrounded by fresh water has no need to save water, so short loops are enough.

questions.q: Streptokinase, an enzyme obtained from Streptococcus bacteria, is used medically to:
o: Dissolve blood clots, for example after a heart attack
questions.x: Streptokinase activates the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin, so it breaks down clots blocking the coronary arteries. It is not an antibiotic.

questions.q: After a labelled probe is added to the sample DNA, any probe that has not paired is washed off. This is done so that:
o: Any signal left comes only from probe bound to the target sequence
The sample DNA is copied many times
The probe is converted into protein
questions.x: Washing removes loose probe; only probe held by complementary base pairing remains. A signal then shows that the target sequence is present in the sample.

questions.q: In a viral-vector vaccine, a harmless virus is used to:
o: Carry a gene for an antigen of another pathogen into body cells
questions.x: The vector virus is modified so it cannot cause disease, and it carries a gene for the target pathogen's antigen. Body cells make that antigen, which stimulates an immune response.

questions.q: Propane burns as C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. What volume of oxygen at STP is needed to burn 4.4 g of propane completely? (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.x: Moles of propane = 4.4/44 = 0.1 mol; O₂ needed = 5 × 0.1 = 0.5 mol = 0.5 × 22.4 = 11.2 dm³. 6.72 dm³ is the volume of CO₂ formed, not O₂ used.

questions.q: A student obtains 12 g of a product, which is an 80% yield. What was the theoretical yield?
questions.x: Theoretical = actual ÷ (percentage/100) = 12 ÷ 0.8 = 15 g. 9.6 g comes from multiplying 12 by 0.8 instead of dividing.

questions.q: Equal masses (8 g each) of hydrogen and oxygen are mixed and sparked: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Which statement is correct? (H = 1, O = 16)
o: Oxygen is limiting and most of the hydrogen is left unreacted
Hydrogen is limiting and most of the oxygen is left unreacted
Both are used up completely because their masses are equal
Hydrogen is limiting because two moles of it are needed
questions.x: H₂ = 8/2 = 4 mol, needing 2 mol O₂; O₂ = 8/32 = 0.25 mol only. So oxygen runs out first and 4 − 0.5 = 3.5 mol of H₂ remains.

questions.q: The orbital concept is needed because a moving electron behaves both as a particle and as a wave. This dual nature of the electron was proposed by:
questions.x: de Broglie suggested that moving particles such as electrons have wave properties (λ = h/mv). Heisenberg gave the uncertainty principle.

questions.q: Electrons falling to the fourth orbit (n = 4) of hydrogen from higher orbits produce the:
questions.x: The series are named by the lower orbit: n = 1 Lyman, 2 Balmer, 3 Paschen, 4 Brackett, 5 Pfund.

questions.q: A general formula giving how many orbitals any subshell contains, in terms of l, is:
questions.x: m runs from −l to +l, which is 2l + 1 values, each one orbital: s 1, p 3, d 5, f 7.

questions.q: Which pair of conditions is NOT the same as STP?
questions.x: STP is 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm (760 mm Hg or 101325 Pa). 25 °C is room temperature, not standard temperature.

questions.q: Which postulate of the kinetic molecular theory explains why a gas spreads out to fill any container it is placed in?
o: Its molecules are attracted strongly to the walls of the container
Its molecules move continuously and randomly in all directions
Its molecules lose energy every time they collide
Its molecules are packed closely together in fixed positions
questions.x: Because gas molecules are in constant random motion in every direction, they spread through the whole space available. Gas molecules are far apart, not packed, and their collisions are elastic.

questions.q: Molecules in a gas have a spread of speeds. When the temperature is raised, the fraction of molecules moving at high speeds:
o: Decreases, while the average speed increases
Stays the same, while the average speed increases
Increases, and the average speed also increases
Increases, but the average speed stays the same
questions.x: Heating shifts the whole speed distribution towards higher values: more molecules move fast and the average speed rises. Some molecules still move slowly, but fewer than before.

questions.q: Which hydrogen halide shows hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
questions.x: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (F, O or N). Among the halogens only fluorine qualifies.

questions.q: Glass softens gradually over a range of temperature instead of melting sharply. The best explanation is that in glass:
o: Particles are held only by ionic bonds of equal strength
Particles are arranged in a perfect three-dimensional lattice
There are no attractive forces between the particles
Particles have only short-range order, so attractions of different strengths break at different temperatures
questions.x: In an amorphous solid the particles are not all in identical surroundings, so the forces holding them are broken over a range of temperature. A perfect lattice would melt sharply.

questions.q: Naphthalene (moth balls) slowly disappears at room temperature without melting. This happens because:
o: Its ions escape from the lattice into the air
It reacts with oxygen of the air
Its covalent bonds break at room temperature
The van der Waals forces between its molecules are weak, so it sublimes
questions.x: Naphthalene forms a molecular crystal held by weak intermolecular forces, so molecules leave the solid directly as vapour (sublimation).

questions.q: Extra reactant is added to an equilibrium mixture at constant temperature. After equilibrium is re-established, the value of Kc:
questions.x: Changing a concentration shifts the position of equilibrium, but Kc changes only with temperature.

questions.q: The solubility of lead(II) chloride, PbCl₂, in water is lowered by adding:
questions.x: KCl supplies Cl⁻, an ion common to PbCl₂, which shifts PbCl₂ ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ to the left. Nitrates share no ion with PbCl₂.

questions.q: The buffer capacity of a CH₃COOH / CH₃COONa buffer is greatest when:
questions.x: A buffer resists added acid and added base best when the acid and its salt are present in equal amounts (pH = pKa). Without either one, it cannot buffer at all.

questions.q: Which of the following reactions is very slow at room temperature?
o: Precipitation of BaSO₄ on mixing BaCl₂(aq) and Na₂SO₄(aq)
Rusting of iron in moist air
Reaction of sodium metal with water
questions.x: Rusting takes days to months. Neutralisation and ionic precipitation are practically instantaneous, and sodium reacts with water vigorously.

questions.q: A small amount of glycerine is added to hydrogen peroxide solution to slow down its decomposition during storage. Glycerine acts as:
o: A reactant that is used up
questions.x: A negative catalyst or inhibitor decreases the rate of a reaction. Glycerine is the standard textbook example for H₂O₂.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands at constant temperature, so its internal energy does not change. It absorbs 250 J of heat. Which is correct? (ΔE = q + w)
o: The gas does 250 J of work on the surroundings
The gas does 500 J of work on the surroundings
250 J of work is done on the gas
questions.x: ΔE = 0, so w = −q = −250 J. A negative w means 250 J of work is done by the gas: all the heat taken in is used for expansion.

questions.q: Which set of quantities are ALL measured in joules?
questions.x: Heat, work and internal energy are all forms or amounts of energy, so their unit is the joule. Heat capacity is in J K⁻¹ and pressure in pascals.

questions.q: Which of the following is the largest amount of energy? (1 cal = 4.184 J)
questions.x: 1 kJ = 1000 J; 100 cal = 418.4 J; 10⁹ erg = 10⁹/10⁷ = 100 J; so 1 kJ is the largest.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares a galvanic (voltaic) cell with an electrolytic cell?
o: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy; an electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a reaction
Both convert electrical energy into chemical energy
A galvanic cell needs an external battery to work
In an electrolytic cell the reaction is spontaneous
questions.x: A galvanic cell produces electricity from a spontaneous reaction; an electrolytic cell is driven by an external source to cause a non-spontaneous change.

questions.q: When molten sodium chloride is electrolysed, sodium metal is produced at the:
questions.x: Na⁺ ions gain electrons at the cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na. Chlorine gas forms at the anode.

questions.q: The rule "like dissolves like" means that:
o: Ionic solutes dissolve only in non-polar solvents
A solute dissolves only in a solvent of the same molar mass
Polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents, and non-polar solutes in non-polar solvents
questions.x: Substances with similar intermolecular forces mix well. Polar or ionic substances dissolve in polar solvents like water; non-polar ones dissolve in solvents like benzene or hexane.

questions.q: The two CH₃ groups in ethane can rotate freely about the C–C bond because:
o: The C–C bond contains a pi bond
The carbon atoms are sp² hybridised
Ethane has lone pairs on each carbon atom
The overlap of a sigma bond is symmetrical about the bond axis
questions.x: A σ bond is cylindrically symmetrical, so rotating one end does not reduce the overlap. A π bond would be broken by rotation, which is why C=C bonds do not rotate freely.

questions.q: Which of these molecules has a net dipole moment?
questions.x: CHCl₃ is tetrahedral but has one C–H bond and three C–Cl bonds, so the bond dipoles do not cancel. The other three are symmetrical and non-polar.

questions.q: Across a period from left to right, the first ionisation energy of the elements generally:
o: First decreases and then stays constant
questions.x: Nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so the outer electrons are held more tightly and are harder to remove.

questions.q: Silicon dioxide dissolves in hot concentrated sodium hydroxide to form sodium silicate, Na₂SiO₃. This shows that SiO₂ is:
o: An amphoteric oxide that reacts only with acids
questions.x: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O: reacting with a base to form a salt and water is the behaviour of an acidic oxide.

questions.q: Titanium has atomic number 22. The electronic configuration of a gaseous Ti²⁺ ion is:
questions.x: Ti is [Ar] 3d² 4s². On ionisation the 4s electrons are lost first, so Ti²⁺ is [Ar] 3d². Keeping 4s² and removing the 3d electrons is the common mistake.

questions.q: In trans-but-2-ene, the two methyl groups are:
o: On the same side of the C=C double bond
Both attached to the same carbon atom
At the two ends of a carbon ring
On opposite sides of the C=C double bond
questions.x: Trans means 'across': the CH₃ groups lie on opposite sides. In cis-but-2-ene they lie on the same side.

questions.q: Ethene is passed into chlorine water (containing HOCl). The organic product is:
questions.x: HOCl adds across the double bond, putting Cl on one carbon and OH on the other: ClCH₂CH₂OH, ethylene chlorohydrin.

questions.q: 13 g of ethyne is hydrated completely with dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄. What mass of ethanal, CH₃CHO, is formed? (C 12, H 1, O 16)
questions.x: Moles of C₂H₂ = 13/26 = 0.5. One mole gives one mole of CH₃CHO (M = 44), so mass = 0.5 × 44 = 22 g.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with chloroethane, C₂H₅Cl, in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The organic product is:
questions.x: This is Friedel–Crafts alkylation: an ethyl group replaces one ring H, giving C₆H₅C₂H₅ and HCl.

questions.q: Which equation is the first propagation step in the chlorination of methane?
questions.x: In propagation a radical reacts with a molecule to give a new radical: Cl• removes H from CH₄, forming HCl and CH₃•. Splitting Cl₂ is initiation; the radical–radical steps are termination.

questions.q: But-2-ene exists as separate cis and trans forms, but butane does not. This is because:
o: But-2-ene has more carbon atoms than butane
Rotation about the C=C double bond is restricted
Butane has a π bond that can rotate freely
The carbons of but-2-ene are sp³ hybridised
questions.x: Restricted rotation about C=C fixes groups on the same side or opposite sides, giving geometric (cis–trans) isomers. In butane, rotation about the C–C σ bonds is free.

questions.q: Ethyne reacts with sodamide, NaNH₂. The products are:
questions.x: The strong base NH₂⁻ removes the acidic H⁺ from ethyne: HC≡CH + NaNH₂ → HC≡CNa + NH₃.

questions.q: 1-chlorobutane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl, is heated with alcoholic KOH. The organic product is:
questions.x: Alcoholic KOH removes HCl from the carbon carrying Cl and its neighbour, giving CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂. Aqueous KOH would give the alcohol instead.

questions.q: Chloropropane, C₃H₇Cl, can exist as how many structural isomers?
questions.x: Chlorine can be on an end carbon (1-chloropropane) or the middle carbon (2-chloropropane). Putting it on the other end carbon gives the same 1-chloropropane again.

questions.q: For the carbon–halogen bonds, the correct order of bond strength (bond enthalpy) is:
questions.x: As the halogen atom gets larger, the C–X bond gets longer and weaker, so C–F is the strongest and C–I the weakest. The reversed order is the common slip.

questions.q: Which of the following dissolves in aqueous sodium hydroxide by forming a salt?
questions.x: 2-Methylphenol (o-cresol) is a phenol, acidic enough to react with NaOH to form a sodium phenoxide salt. Cyclohexanol, benzyl alcohol and ethanol are alcohols and do not react with aqueous NaOH.

questions.q: The esterification of ethanol with ethanoic acid is reversible. The yield of ethyl ethanoate can be increased by:
o: Using dilute instead of concentrated H₂SO₄
questions.x: Adding excess of a reactant shifts the equilibrium towards the products. Adding water pushes it back towards the reactants, and a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium at all.

questions.q: When propanal is reduced to propan-1-ol, how many hydrogen atoms are added to each molecule?
questions.x: CH₃CH₂CHO (C₃H₆O) becomes CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (C₃H₈O): one H goes to the carbonyl carbon and one to the oxygen, two H atoms in all.

questions.q: A ketone carrying two very bulky alkyl groups, such as (CH₃)₃CCOC(CH₃)₃, adds nucleophiles extremely slowly. This is mainly because:
o: The carbonyl carbon carries a large positive charge
The C=O bond in it is non-polar
The bulky groups hinder the approach of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon
questions.x: Large groups crowd the carbonyl carbon (steric hindrance) and also release electrons, so a nucleophile approaches with difficulty. This is the same effect, in a stronger form, that makes ketones less reactive than aldehydes.

questions.q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethanol at room temperature. The products are:
questions.x: CH₃COCl + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + HCl. Unlike esterification of the acid, this reaction is fast and goes to completion.

questions.q: Antibodies, which help defend the body against infection, belong chemically to the:
questions.x: Antibodies are soluble, globular proteins (immunoglobulins) in blood plasma. Keratins are structural fibrous proteins.

questions.q: In a dye molecule, the main role of an auxochrome group such as –OH or –NH₂ is to:
o: Supply the colour on its own without a chromophore
Make the dye insoluble in water
Reduce the dye to a colourless form
Deepen the colour and help the dye attach to the fibre
questions.x: The chromophore is responsible for colour; the auxochrome intensifies it and gives the dye a group that can bind to the fibre. Without a chromophore there is no colour.

questions.q: Work out the cross product (î + ĵ) × (î − ĵ):
questions.x: For vectors in the xy-plane, the cross product is (PxQy − PyQx)k̂ = (1 × (−1) − 1 × 1)k̂ = −2k̂.

questions.q: Two vectors P and Q are inclined at an angle θ. The magnitude of their vector product is:
questions.x: |P × Q| = PQ sin θ. PQ cos θ is the scalar product.

questions.q: Launch angles of 30° and 60° with equal speed give equal ranges on level ground. How do their flight times compare (30° : 60°)?
questions.x: Time of flight = 2v sin θ / g, so the ratio is sin 30° : sin 60° = ½ : √3/2 = 1 : √3. Their ranges are equal, but their times are not.

questions.q: An aeroplane flying horizontally at 100 m s⁻¹ at a height of 500 m releases a packet. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the packet travels a horizontal distance before landing of:
questions.x: Time to fall: 500 = ½ × 10 × t², so t = 10 s. The horizontal velocity stays 100 m s⁻¹, so distance = 100 × 10 = 1000 m.

questions.q: During a collision, body X exerts force F on body Y, and Y exerts −F on X for the same time. This shows that the total momentum is conserved because:
o: The impulses on the two bodies are equal and opposite, so their momentum changes cancel
The forces act on the same body and cancel
The kinetic energy of each body stays the same
questions.x: Each body receives an impulse F × t, equal in size and opposite in direction, so one gains exactly the momentum the other loses.

questions.q: A runner goes once along a semicircular track of radius 7 m, from one end of the diameter to the other, in 2 s. Taking π = 22/7, her average speed and the magnitude of her average velocity are:
questions.x: Distance = πr = 22 m, so average speed = 22 ÷ 2 = 11 m s⁻¹. Displacement = diameter = 14 m, so average velocity = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: If air resistance is NOT ignored, the horizontal component of a projectile's velocity:
o: Becomes zero at the highest point
questions.x: Air resistance acts against the motion and has a backward horizontal part, so the horizontal component falls. It stays constant only when air resistance is ignored.

questions.q: A force acts on a moving body at right angles to its velocity at every instant. The power delivered by this force is:
questions.x: P = F·v = Fv cos θ. With θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so the force delivers no power and does no work.

questions.q: An LED bulb and a filament bulb give the same amount of light, but the LED uses much less electrical power. This is because the LED:
o: Produces more heat than the filament bulb
Does not obey the law of conservation of energy
Stores the extra energy inside it
Wastes less energy as heat, so it is more efficient
questions.x: Both give the same useful light output, but the filament bulb turns most of its input into heat. The LED wastes less, so its efficiency is higher.

questions.q: A 4 kg body has 50 J of kinetic energy. Its speed is:
questions.x: ½ × 4 × v² = 50, so v² = 25 and v = 5 m s⁻¹. 25 m s⁻¹ forgets to take the square root.

questions.q: Taking one rotation of the Earth as 24 hours, through what angle does the Earth turn about its axis in 4 hours?
questions.x: In 4 hours the Earth makes 4/24 = 1/6 of a turn, so it turns 2π/6 = π/3 rad.

questions.q: A ceiling fan rotates at 300 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is:
questions.x: 300 rev min⁻¹ = 5 rev s⁻¹; ω = 2π × 5 = 10π rad s⁻¹. Forgetting the 2π gives 5 rad s⁻¹.

questions.q: A glass bead settles through glycerine at a steady 4 cm s⁻¹. Another bead, equal in size but made of a material of double the density, would settle at: (take v_t ∝ ρ, ignoring upthrust)
questions.x: v_t is directly proportional to the density ρ of the sphere, so doubling ρ doubles v_t: 2 × 4 = 8 cm s⁻¹. It is the radius, not the density, that enters as a square.

questions.q: A level Venturi meter has a 4 cm² inlet and a 2 cm² throat. Water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³) enters at 2 m s⁻¹. How much higher is the pressure at the inlet than at the throat?
questions.x: By continuity the throat speed is 4 m s⁻¹. ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = 500 × (16 − 4) = 6000 Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 12 000 Pa.

questions.q: A steel ball falls at its terminal velocity through a tall jar of oil. The gravitational potential energy it loses is mainly converted into:
o: Extra kinetic energy of the ball
Internal (heat) energy of the oil and ball, through work done against drag
Elastic potential energy stored in the oil
questions.x: The ball's speed, and so its kinetic energy, is constant at terminal velocity. The energy lost goes into work against the viscous drag, which warms the oil and ball.

questions.q: The adiabatic bulk modulus of air is larger than its isothermal bulk modulus. The reason is that in an adiabatic compression:
o: The temperature rises, so the pressure rises more for the same decrease in volume
The temperature falls, so the air becomes easier to compress
Heat flows in from the surroundings, keeping the temperature fixed
The density of the air stays constant
questions.x: In a rapid (adiabatic) compression no heat escapes, so the air warms and its pressure rises more than in an isothermal compression. A larger pressure rise for the same volume change means a larger modulus, γP instead of P.

questions.q: At the same temperature, sound travels faster in helium than in argon (both monatomic, so with the same γ). The reason is that helium:
o: Has a much smaller molar mass, so it is less dense at the same pressure
Has a much larger molar mass
Is a better conductor of heat
Exerts a higher pressure at the same temperature
questions.x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(γRT/M). At the same T and γ, the gas with the smaller molar mass (helium, 4 g mol⁻¹, against 40 for argon) carries sound faster.

questions.q: A ship's sonar sends a pulse of sound down to the sea bed. The echo returns after 2.0 s. If sound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹ in sea water, the depth of the sea is:
questions.x: The pulse travels down and back, so depth = (1500 × 2.0)/2 = 1500 m. Forgetting to halve gives 3000 m.

questions.q: Waves from an earthquake travel through the rocks of the Earth. These waves are:
o: Electromagnetic waves, because they travel very fast
Electromagnetic waves, because they can cross empty space
Mechanical waves, because they need the rock as a medium
questions.x: Seismic waves are vibrations of the rock itself, so they are mechanical waves that need a medium. They cannot cross a vacuum.

questions.q: Which description fits an antinode of a stationary wave?
o: A point where the displacement is always zero
A point where the particles never move
A point where the amplitude of vibration is maximum
A point where the wave changes its frequency
questions.x: At an antinode the particles vibrate with the largest amplitude. The point of zero displacement at all times is a node.

questions.q: In which type of wave do the pressure and density of the medium rise and fall from point to point along the wave?
questions.x: A longitudinal wave is a train of compressions (high pressure and density) and rarefactions (low pressure and density). A string wave displaces particles sideways, and light needs no medium.

questions.q: Hot water at 80 °C is added to 1 kg of cold water at 20 °C until the mixture reaches 40 °C. Ignoring heat losses, the mass of hot water added is:
questions.x: Heat lost = heat gained: m × c × (80 − 40) = 1 × c × (40 − 20), so 40m = 20 and m = 0.5 kg.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands isothermally from volume V to 2V, starting at pressure P. Compared with P × V, the work done by the gas is:
o: Less than P × V, because the pressure falls during the expansion
Equal to P × V, because the temperature is constant
Greater than P × V, because the volume doubles
Zero, because the temperature does not change
questions.x: P × V would be the work if the pressure stayed at P. In isothermal expansion the pressure falls from P to P/2, so the area under the curve is less than PV.

questions.q: A gas takes in 900 J of heat, but its internal energy goes up by only 500 J. The rest leaves as work done by the gas, equal to:
questions.x: Q = ΔU + W, with W the work done by the gas: 900 = 500 + W, so W = 400 J.

questions.q: A point charge q produces a field of magnitude E at distance r. A charge 2q at distance 2r produces a field of magnitude:
questions.x: E = kq/r². Doubling q doubles E and doubling r divides it by 4, so the new field is 2/4 = E/2.

questions.q: The electric field due to an isolated positive point charge points:
o: Radially outward, away from the charge
Parallel to a fixed direction everywhere
questions.x: A positive test charge is repelled by a positive charge, so the field points radially away from it. Towards the charge is the case for a negative charge.

questions.q: A positive charge is moved, by an external agent, in the direction opposite to the electric field. Its electric potential energy:
questions.x: Moving a positive charge against the field requires work by the agent, which is stored as an increase in electric potential energy, like lifting a mass against gravity.

questions.q: A cell drives a current of 1 A through a 4 Ω resistor and 0.5 A through a 10 Ω resistor. The emf of the cell is:
questions.x: E = I(R + r): E = 1(4 + r) and E = 0.5(10 + r). So 4 + r = 5 + 0.5r, giving r = 2 Ω and E = 6 V.

questions.q: The internal resistance of a cell is the resistance offered by:
o: The connecting wires of the external circuit
The load connected to the cell
The electrolyte and electrodes inside the cell
The voltmeter connected across the cell
questions.x: Charges flowing through the cell itself meet resistance from its electrolyte and electrodes; this is the internal resistance r.

questions.q: At a point in a magnetic field, the direction of the flux density vector is the direction in which:
o: The north pole of a small compass needle points
A stationary positive charge would be pushed
The south pole of a small compass needle points
questions.x: B points along the field lines, the way a compass north pole points. A stationary charge feels no magnetic force, and the force on a wire is perpendicular to B.

questions.q: Power sent along a line is P = VI. For a fixed power, raising the transmission voltage makes the line current:
questions.x: I = P/V, so for the same power a higher voltage means a smaller current.

questions.q: An electromagnetic wave in a vacuum has a frequency of 1.5 × 10⁸ Hz (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Its wavelength and its region of the spectrum are:
questions.x: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸/(1.5 × 10⁸) = 2 m, which lies in the radio-wave region. Infrared has wavelengths below a millimetre, and dividing f by c gives 0.5 m instead.

questions.q: A hole in a p-type semiconductor is best described as:
o: A free proton that moves through the crystal
A vacancy left where an electron is missing from a covalent bond, acting as a positive charge
A negative ion fixed in the crystal lattice
An extra electron supplied by the impurity atom
questions.x: A hole is a missing electron in a bond. Neighbouring electrons can move into it, so the hole moves and behaves like a positive carrier; it is not a proton.

questions.q: A laser emits 2 × 10¹⁸ photons per second, each of energy 3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Its power output is:
questions.x: Power = number per second × energy each = 2 × 10¹⁸ × 3 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.6 W.

questions.q: The lines of the Brackett series of hydrogen are produced by transitions that end on the level:
questions.x: Lyman ends on n = 1, Balmer on n = 2, Paschen on n = 3, Brackett on n = 4 and Pfund on n = 5.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a medical use of radioisotopes?
questions.x: Carbon-14 dating is used in archaeology to find the age of remains, not for diagnosis or treatment. The others are standard medical uses.

questions.q: When the coach read out the team for the final, Hamza's name was not on the list. He said nothing, packed his kit slowly, and told his friends he had a headache and wanted to go home. That evening his mother found his new football boots pushed to the very back of the cupboard. What does the passage suggest?
o: Hamza was too ill to play in the final
Hamza had decided to buy better boots
Hamza did not care about the final
Hamza was deeply disappointed at not being chosen
questions.x: His silence, slow packing and hidden boots show hurt at being left out; the headache is an excuse to leave. Hiding the boots shows he cared, so 'did not care' is wrong.

questions.q: In which sentence is hyperbole used?
o: "This bag weighs a ton; I can hardly lift it."
"The bag was as heavy as a sack of wheat."
"The heavy bag groaned at its seams."
"The bag was heavy, so Ali carried it slowly."
questions.x: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration: a bag one can carry does not really weigh a ton. The 'as heavy as' line is a simile, the 'groaned' line is personification, and the last is literal.

questions.q: A guard shouts one word at a boy. Which version of the sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.x: The exclamation mark belongs to the spoken word, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark, and no extra comma is added after it.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "Sara does not know ___ to the new hospital."
questions.x: A question word such as 'how' can be followed by a to-infinitive: 'how to get'.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "In no way ___ responsible for the accident."
questions.x: After the negative phrase 'In no way', the verb 'is' moves before the subject; 'does' cannot be used with an adjective like 'responsible'.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "Please let him ___ his own way home."
questions.x: 'Let' is followed by the object and the bare infinitive (without 'to').

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: "By next June, Ali ___ his FSc examinations."
questions.x: 'By' with a future time takes the future perfect, for an action finished before that time.

questions.q: Report in indirect speech: The captain said to the players, "Play as a team."
o: The captain told the players that play as a team.
The captain said the players to play as a team.
The captain told the players that they play as a team.
The captain told the players to play as a team.
questions.x: A command is reported with 'told' + object + to-infinitive.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "A box of pencils ____ been placed on each desk."
questions.x: The subject is 'a box', which is singular; 'of pencils' only describes it. So the verb is 'has been placed'.

questions.q: Records show that elderly people who use walking sticks fall more often than those who do not. Someone concludes that walking sticks cause falls. What is the main flaw?
o: Walking sticks are made of wood, which is slippery
Elderly people never fall without a reason
People who are already unsteady on their feet are the ones more likely to use sticks
Only a few elderly people use walking sticks
questions.x: The link may run the other way: poor balance leads people to use sticks, and poor balance also causes falls. The stick need not be the cause.

questions.q: An advertisement shows ten students who used a certain guidebook and got into medical college. What is the main flaw in using this as proof that the book works?
o: Medical colleges do not allow guidebooks
It shows only the successful users and ignores those who did not get in
The students may have bought the book from different shops
questions.x: Picking only the successes hides how many users failed. Without the full picture, ten success stories prove nothing about the book.

questions.q: Find the next term: B4, D8, F12, H16, ?
questions.x: The letters skip one (B, D, F, H, J) and each number is double the letter's position: J is 10th, so J20.

questions.q: Find the next letter: K, M, J, N, I, O, ?
questions.x: Two series are mixed: K, J, I (going back one) and M, N, O (going forward one). The seventh term belongs to the first series, so it is H.

questions.q: Bilal is older than Hamza but younger than Ali. Who is the oldest of the three?
questions.x: The order is Ali, then Bilal, then Hamza from oldest to youngest, so Ali is the oldest.

questions.q: Four sisters, Aiza, Bisma, Dua and Eman, each play a different sport: badminton, cricket, hockey or tennis. Aiza plays neither cricket nor tennis. Bisma plays hockey. Dua does not play cricket. Who plays cricket?
questions.x: With hockey taken by Bisma, Aiza must play badminton. Dua does not play cricket, so she plays tennis, and Eman plays cricket.

questions.q: Statement: A hospital's records show that most patient falls in its wards happen at night after the lights are switched off. Courses of action: I. Dim night lights should be provided in the wards. II. Patients should not be allowed to get out of bed at all. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: The data link falls to darkness, so dim night lights address the cause. Keeping every patient in bed at all times is impractical and harmful.

questions.q: Statement: One student in a class developed a rash after using a new brand of soap. Courses of action: I. That brand of soap should be banned across the country. II. All students in the class should stop washing their hands. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: One rash in one person is not enough to ban a product nationwide, and stopping handwashing would harm health. Neither action follows.

questions.q: In a town, people who own more books tend to live longer. Someone concludes that owning books makes people live longer. Which fact, if true, best shows the flaw in this conclusion?
o: Books are sold in many shops in the town
Some people borrow books from the library
Reading can be done at any age
Wealthier families both buy more books and can afford better health care
questions.x: Wealth could cause both more books and longer lives, so the books need not be the cause. A third factor can create a link between two things.
